level1.text: The average power of a wind turbine over a week ($168\,\text{h}$) is $2.5\,\text{MW}$. How much electricity does it produce in a week? Give the answer in megawatt-hours.

A hydropower plant runs for $8.0\,\text{h}$ at a power of $120\,\text{MW}$ when the consumption of electricity is high in the evening. How much energy does the plant produce during this time? Give the answer in megawatt-hours.
The power of the Olkiluoto 3 nuclear power plant is $1.6\,\text{GW}$. How much energy does the plant produce in a day when it runs at this power all the time? Give the answer in gigawatt-hours.

The bar chart in the figure shows electricity production in Finland in 2024 by energy source (Statistics Finland). Total production was $79.9\,\text{TWh}$. Read from the figure the production of the weather-dependent sources, wind power and solar power. What percentage of the electricity did they produce together?

The power of the solar panels of a detached house in the middle of a summer day is $4.0\,\text{kW}$. How much electricity do the panels produce in $3.5\,\text{h}$, when the power stays the same? Give the answer in kilowatt-hours.
Which of the following energy sources is renewable?

choices.feedback: Uranium is not renewable: there is a limited amount of uranium ore, and no more of it forms on a human timescale. Nuclear power produced with uranium still does not emit carbon dioxide during operation.
Coal is not renewable: it formed over millions of years, and no more forms at the rate at which it is burned. Burning it releases carbon dioxide.
Correct: the Sun keeps heating the atmosphere, so the energy of the wind can be used without it running out. Wind is still weather-dependent, so renewable does not always mean available.
Natural gas is not renewable: it is a fossil fuel that formed over millions of years. Burning it releases carbon dioxide.

level1.text: In an electricity grid, production and consumption must be equal at every moment. What is meant by regulating power?
level1.answer: A power plant whose power can be changed quickly, such as a hydropower plant.

choices.text: A power plant whose power can be changed quickly, such as a hydropower plant.
choices.feedback: Correct: regulating power is production whose power can be changed as needed. The power of a hydropower plant can be increased or decreased quickly by adjusting the flow, which is why it suits balancing the variation of wind power.

choices.text: A power plant that produces steadily all year, such as a nuclear power plant.
choices.feedback: A plant that produces steadily is base load power. Its power is usually not changed to follow consumption, so it is not regulating power.

choices.text: A power plant whose power varies with the weather, such as a wind turbine.
choices.feedback: The power of a weather-dependent plant varies, but it cannot be chosen: wind and sun do not obey consumption. With regulating power the power is changed on purpose, which is why weather-dependent production needs regulating power alongside it.

level1.text: The rated power of an example wind turbine is $4.0\,\text{MW}$, and it produces $11\,\text{GWh}$ of electricity in a year. For how many hours would the turbine have to run at its rated power to produce the same energy? Give the answer in hours.

A wind turbine has a rated power of $3.0\,\text{MW}$, and its average power over a year is $33\,\%$ of the rated power.

The electricity consumption of a detached house is $5000\,\text{kWh}$ per year.

Approximately how many detached houses' annual consumption does the turbine produce in a year ($8760\,\text{h}$)? Choose the closest value.

choices.feedback: This results when the turbine's annual energy in megawatt-hours, $8700\,\text{MWh}$, is divided by the house's consumption $5000$ without converting the units. A megawatt-hour is a thousand kilowatt-hours, so the number is a thousand times too small.
This results when the share $33\,\%$ is misread as a tenth, about $3.3\,\%$. The share $33\,\%$ is $0.33$, so the average power is about a third of the rated power, not a thirtieth.

Correct: the average power is $0.33 \cdot 3.0\,\text{MW} \approx 1\,\text{MW}$, that is $1000\,\text{kW}$, the annual energy is about $1000\,\text{kW} \cdot 8760\,\text{h}$, that is about $8.7 \cdot 10^{6}\,\text{kWh}$, and $8.7 \cdot 10^{6} : 5000 \approx 1700$, which is of the order of $2000$.

This results when the rated power $3.0\,\text{MW}$ is used instead of the average power $0.33 \cdot 3.0\,\text{MW}$. Then the annual energy is about $2.6 \cdot 10^{7}\,\text{kWh}$ and the number of houses is about $5000$. However, the turbine does not produce at its rated power all year because the wind does not blow all the time, so the annual energy is calculated with the average power.

level2.text: An example wind farm has a rated power of $25\,\text{MW}$, and its average power over the year is $32\,\%$ of the rated power. How much electricity does the farm produce in a year, when a year has $8760\,\text{h}$? Give the answer in gigawatt-hours.

Finnish hydropower produced about $14\,\text{TWh}$ of electricity in 2024 (Statistics Finland). For how many hours would Olkiluoto 3 ($1.6\,\text{GW}$) have to run at full power to produce the same energy? Give the answer in hours.

Nuclear power plants produced about $31\,\text{TWh}$ of electricity in 2024. An example wind turbine produces $12\,\text{GWh}$ in a year. How many such wind turbines would be needed to produce the same annual energy as the nuclear power plants produced?

Olkiluoto 3 ($1.6\,\text{GW}$) runs at full power for the whole year ($8760\,\text{h}$). An example household without electric heating uses $5000\,\text{kWh}$ in a year. How many households' annual consumption would the plant cover? Give the answer in millions of households.

The table gives, as example figures (an example data set, not the statistics of a real country), the electricity production of a country by source in two years ten years apart. Calculate the share of wind power in the total production for both years and the change in the share. Give the answer as the change in percentage points. Whose energy decreased the most, and what does this tell about the change in the production structure?

level2.text:
The table gives, as example figures (an example data set), the rated power and the energy produced during a year for three wind farms. A student says: “Farm B produces the most electricity, so it makes the best use of its rated power.”

a) For each farm, calculate how large a share of the rated power is in use on average, when a year has $8760\,\text{h}$.

b) Is the student right? What is the error in the student's reasoning? Answer in the box with the average power of the best farm as a percentage of its rated power.

level2.text:
The table gives, as example figures (an example data set), the life-cycle emissions of four production methods, that is, the amount of carbon dioxide produced over the whole life cycle per kilowatt-hour of electricity produced, and the lifetime of the plant. An example city uses $2.0\,\text{TWh}$ of electricity per year.

a) Take the part of the life-cycle emissions that belongs to one year's electricity production. How many million tonnes of carbon dioxide per year would be saved if the city's electricity were produced with wind power instead of coal? Use the emission factors and convert $1\,\text{t} = 10^{6}\,\text{g}$.

b) Which production method would be the best choice on the basis of emissions and lifetime? What does the table not tell, even though the choice would have to be made?

data.caption: Life-cycle emissions and lifetime of production methods

level3.text: An example frosty evening: the consumption of electricity in Finland is $11\,\text{GW}$. Nuclear power plants run at a power of $3.5\,\text{GW}$. The combined rated power of wind turbines is $9.0\,\text{GW}$, but the wind is weak and they produce only $4.0\,\%$ of their rated power. How much power must other power plants and imported electricity produce? Give the answer in gigawatts.

An example wind farm and nuclear power plant have the same rated power, $600\,\text{MW}$. The average power of the wind farm is $33\,\%$ and that of the nuclear power plant $90\,\%$ of the rated power. How many times as much energy does the nuclear power plant produce in a year? Give the answer as a factor.

An example municipality proposes a solar park that would replace Olkiluoto 3 ($1600\,\text{MW}$). The average power of the solar park over the year is $11\,\%$ and that of Olkiluoto 3 $90\,\%$ of the rated power.

How large should the rated power of the solar park be for it to produce as much energy in a year as Olkiluoto 3? Give the answer in gigawatts. Also consider whether such a park would replace Olkiluoto 3 on a January evening.

The table gives, as example figures (an example data set), the average wind power and the electricity consumption for each day of a week. The total rated power of the wind turbines is $9.0\,\text{GW}$. Nuclear power plants produce a steady $3.5\,\text{GW}$ for the whole week. Assume that other production and imports cover what wind and nuclear power leave uncovered.

a) Calculate the energy produced by wind power in the week in gigawatt-hours and the average power of wind power as a percentage of the rated power.

b) For each day, calculate the power that other power plants and imports must produce. Answer in the box with the greatest such power in gigawatts.

c) What does the variation of wind power require of the rest of the electricity system? Justify with the numbers in the table, and also comment on Sunday.

data.caption: Wind power and electricity consumption during a week

level3.text:
A municipality is comparing two ways of producing electricity. The table gives, as example figures (an example data set, not data of real projects), the details of a wind farm and a nuclear power plant. Assume that each plant produces the same amount of energy every year during its whole lifetime as in the first year, and that the cost is only the construction cost. A year has $8760\,\text{h}$.

a) Calculate the annual energy of each plant in megawatt-hours.

b) Calculate the construction cost per megawatt-hour produced over the whole lifetime. Answer in the box with the value of the wind farm in euros per megawatt-hour.

c) For each plant, calculate the amount of carbon dioxide in tonnes that belongs to one year's production from the life-cycle emissions, when $1\,\text{t} = 10^{6}\,\text{g}$.

d) Compare the production methods on the basis of emissions, cost and controllability, and give a justified recommendation.

data.caption: Comparison of a wind farm and a nuclear power plant
